::: {.callout-note}
## About this page

This page **tests how the viewer opens figures of different shapes**:
very wide collages (25 × 2 inches), tall strips, a poster, a portrait
photo and a small plot, each on its own, and the `fit` option. All are
png; other formats are on [E: image formats](e-formats.html), and the same
shapes in galleries and layouts on
[I: wide figures in galleries and layouts](i-wide-galleries.html).

**The rules** (`fit: auto`, the default). The viewer opens most images
whole. A strip at least 3 times wider than tall, that would show less than
a quarter of the screen tall, such as a collage of many panels
(`fig-width: 100`, `fig-height: 5`), opens filling the screen height
instead. A strip at least 3 times taller than wide, that would show less
than a quarter of the screen wide, opens filling the screen width, at its
top. Ordinary photos and plots, portrait or landscape, always open whole,
even on a very wide screen where a portrait photo is narrower than a
quarter of it. No image is enlarged past its real size when it opens (as
with Quarto's lightbox): a small image opens at its own size, and
scrolling still zooms it in, up to `max-zoom`. `fit: contain`, `height` or
`width` overrides the rule for one figure.

**Focal point.** Where you click a strip on the page is its focal point:
click panel 12 of a 20-panel collage and the viewer opens with panel 12 in
the middle of the screen (or flush with the end, near either end). The 0
key and double-click return to it. Opened from the keyboard, a strip
starts at its left end (or top). Ordinary images open whole wherever you
click. Zooming out still shows the whole figure.

Shift+scroll (or a sideways trackpad swipe) pans along the direction the
figure extends past the screen: sideways for a collage, up and down for a
tall figure, sideways when zoomed in both ways.

Headings carry what the browser test checks: `expect-fit` (`contain`,
`height` or `width`), `shift-scroll` (which way Shift+scroll moves the
image: `x` sideways, `y` up and down, `none`, or `zoomed-x`: sideways
after zooming in until the image extends past the screen both ways) and
`expect-scale="1"` (opens at real size), `expect-zoom-out` (`yes`: the
opening view is closer than the whole image, so it zooms out; `no`: it
already is the whole image). The first single collage and
image shown whole also get the focal point and containment checks.
:::

The cases below draw with these helpers:

```{r}
# A collage: `n` panels side by side, like a wide patchwork figure.
collage <- function(n = 12) {
  set.seed(1)
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(cumsum(rnorm(200)), type = "l", main = paste("Panel", i),
         xlab = "", ylab = "", col = hcl.colors(n)[i], lwd = 2)
  }
}

# A tall strip: `n` rows stacked, like a tall patchwork figure.
# Each seed gets its own palette (without its lightest end), so different
# strips look different.
strip <- function(seed = 2, n = 8) {
  set.seed(seed)
  palette <- c("Viridis", "Plasma", "Zissou 1", "Dark 3", "Sunset", "Cividis", "Dynamic", "Inferno")[(seed - 2) %% 8 + 1]
  par(mfrow = c(n, 1), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(cumsum(rnorm(100)), type = "l", main = paste0("Strip ", seed, ", row ", i),
         xlab = "", ylab = "", col = hcl.colors(n + 2, palette)[i], lwd = 2)
  }
}

wave <- function(k = 1) {
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  col <- hcl.colors(4, "Dark 3")[k]
  plot(x, sin(k * x), type = "n", main = paste("Wave", k), xlab = "x", ylab = "sin(kx)")
  polygon(c(x, rev(x)), c(sin(k * x), rep(0, length(x))), col = adjustcolor(col, 0.35), border = NA)
  lines(x, sin(k * x), lwd = 2, col = col)
}
```

## 1. Wide collage, png (25 × 2 in) {#c1 expect-fit="height" shift-scroll="x"}

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 25
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-cap: "A 25 × 2 inch collage of 12 panels (png)."

collage(n = 12)
```

## 2. Wide collage with `fit: contain` {#c2 expect-fit="contain" shift-scroll="none"}

The override for case 1: the whole collage, as a strip.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: contain
#| fig-width: 25
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-cap: "The collage, forced to open whole."

collage(n = 12)
```

## 3. Moderately wide figure (16 × 4 in) {#c3 expect-fit="contain"}

Wide, but readable whole: the size rule leaves it alone.

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "A 4:1 figure."

collage(n = 4)
```

## 4. Tall strip (4 × 15 in) {#c4 expect-fit="width" shift-scroll="y"}

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 15
#| fig-cap: "A tall strip of 8 panels."

strip(seed = 2, n = 8)
```

## 5. Large poster (24 × 18 in) {#c5 expect-fit="contain" shift-scroll="zoomed-x"}

Opens whole; zoomed in, it extends past the screen both ways, and
Shift+scroll moves sideways.

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 24
#| fig-height: 18
#| fig-cap: "A 24 × 18 inch poster of 48 panels."

set.seed(3)
par(mfrow = c(6, 8), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:48) plot(cumsum(rnorm(100)), type = "l", main = paste("Panel", i), xlab = "", ylab = "")
```

## 6. Portrait photo {#c6 expect-fit="contain"}

An ordinary 9:16 photo is not a strip: it opens whole, on any screen width
(the test also checks this in a 2560 px wide window).

![A portrait photo.](../../images/mv-4.jpg){.panzoom width=30%}

## 7. Small plot (288 × 192 px) {#c7 expect-fit="contain" expect-scale="1"}

Opens at its real size, centered, rather than enlarged to fill the
screen; scroll still zooms in (up to `max-zoom`).

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-dpi: 48
#| fig-cap: "A small plot."

plot(pressure)
```

## 8. `fit: height` on an ordinary plot {#c8 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="height" expect-zoom-out="no"}

On a screen wider than the plot (1.4:1), filling the height is already the
whole plot, so this opens like `fit: contain` and can't zoom out. Case 10
shows `fit: height` on a figure where it differs.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height

wave(k = 3)
```

## 9. `fit: width` on an ordinary plot {#c9 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="width" expect-zoom-out="yes"}

Filling the width makes the plot taller than the screen: it opens closer
than the whole plot, and zooms out to it.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: width

wave(k = 4)
```

## 10. `fit: height` on a wide figure (12 × 4.5 in) {#c10 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="height" expect-zoom-out="yes"}

Not a strip (shown whole it is over a quarter of the screen tall), so
`fit: auto` would open it whole. `fit: height` opens it filling the screen
height (but not past its real size), from where it was clicked, and zooms
out to the whole figure.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

collage(n = 6)
```

## 11. Case 10 with a long caption and description {#c11 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="height" expect-zoom-out="yes"}

The caption and description sit below the image; `fit: height` fills the
height left above them, so it opens smaller than case 10. The caption
scrolls past a quarter of the screen, the description past a fifth, so the
image keeps at least about half.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height
#|   description: "A long description, to take room below the image. Each panel is a random walk of 200 steps, drawn with base R's `plot()` in a one-row layout (`par(mfrow = c(1, 6))`), colored along the `hcl.colors()` palette. The figure is 12 by 4.5 inches, which knitr writes at 192 dpi (2304 by 864 px). With `fit: height` the viewer opens it as tall as the space above this text allows, and no taller than its real size. Drag or use the arrow keys to move along the figure, scroll or press - to zoom out to the whole of it, and 0 to come back to this opening view."
#| fig-cap: "Six random walks side by side, opened with `fit: height` under a long description."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

collage(n = 6)
```
